results.claim: An alleged optimum has a linear-time verifiable certificate, even for arbitrary signed entries.
results.proof_sketch: Let q=min(m,n), and let F_l be the maximum sum of an l by l square. Adopt L=0 when no positive length is feasible. Build the two-dimensional prefix-sum table in O(mn) time. A certificate for optimum L consists of: (i) for every l>L, coordinates of one l-square having sum greater than k; and (ii) no additional data for L. Verification checks all (m-L+1)(n-L+1) L-squares have sum at most k (vacuous for L=0), and checks the supplied witness for each l>L. Every sum is obtained from four prefix entries. Thus verification costs O(mn+q)=O(mn). The first condition proves L feasible, while the witnesses prove every larger length infeasible, so the characterization is exact.

results.claim: There is an exact output-sensitive search algorithm whose worst-case time is O(mn min(m,n)).
results.proof_sketch: After prefix-sum preprocessing, inspect lengths q,q-1,...,1. For each l, scan its square placements until finding a sum greater than k; retain that placement as the infeasibility witness. Return the first l for which the entire scan finds no violation, or 0 if every length has a witness. Correctness follows directly from descending order. If m>=n=q, the optimum is L, and d=q-L, the number of tested placements is at most sum_{t=0}^d (m-n+t+1)(t+1), hence the total time is O(mn+(m-n+1)(d+1)^2+(d+1)^3). This is O(mnq) in the worst case and O(mn) whenever d=O(1). When L=0, extending the displayed sum through t=q only adds the harmless side-zero term to the upper bound. The algorithm also constructs the preceding certificate.

results.claim: Feasibility can alternate at every side length, and the natural no-revisit greedy extension is incorrect.
results.proof_sketch: For any n, take an n by n matrix whose first row is 1,-1,1,-1,... and whose other rows are zero, with k=0. For even l, every length-l interval of the first row sums to zero, so every l-square has sum zero. For odd l, the l-square starting in the first row and first column has sum one, while no square has larger sum. Hence F_l=0 for even l and F_l=1 for odd l: feasibility alternates Theta(n) times, ruling out binary search or any interval-monotonicity argument. Separately, with k=1 and matrix [[2,1,1],[-3,1,1]], the two side-2 sums, scanned left to right, are 1 and 4. A greedy scan sees the first as safe, decreases to side 1 only at the second, and sees only entries at most 1 thereafter; without revisiting the first entry it returns 1. This is wrong because the earlier entry 2 makes side 1 infeasible as well, so the true answer under the L=0 convention is 0.

results.claim: Any deterministic exact algorithm in the standard explicit one-word-per-entry cell-probe model requires Omega(mn) input probes in the worst case, even for Boolean matrices and k=0; thus an O(mn) algorithm would be optimal in this model.
results.proof_sketch: Let q=min(m,n) and run the algorithm on the all-zero matrix Z. Its answer is q. Fix any cell (r,c), using zero-based indices. The q-square with top row min(r,m-q) and left column min(c,n-q) is in bounds and contains (r,c); this formula also covers q=1, corners, and the long dimension of a rectangular matrix. If the execution on Z did not probe (r,c), change only that entry to one. Every probed word and hence the entire adaptive execution would be unchanged, but the displayed q-square would have sum one, so q would be infeasible at threshold zero and the correct answer would be less than q. This contradiction forces the zero-input execution to probe all mn cells. The lower bound is unconditional for this explicit-input model and already holds on nonnegative entries; it matches, but does not rule out, the requested O(mn) endpoint.

results.claim: The O(mn) endpoint is achievable for two nontrivial signed separable classes: multiplicative rank one and additive separability.
results.proof_sketch: Suppose first that A_ij=u_i v_j. For each l, let X_l be all length-l window sums of u and Y_l those of v. Every l-square sum is xy with x in X_l and y in Y_l. Its maximum is attained among the four products formed from min X_l, max X_l, min Y_l, and max Y_l. One-dimensional prefix sums compute these extrema in O(m+n) time per l, so all q lengths cost O(q(m+n))<=2mn. A nonzero rank-one matrix is recognized by choosing a nonzero pivot p=A_rc and checking pA_ij=A_ic A_rj everywhere. Using the pivot column and row, each corner candidate is a numerator divided by p; divide each of the four numerators by p before taking their maximum. This candidatewise order is valid also for p<0, whereas moving a negative division outside a maximum would reverse extrema. The all-zero case is immediate. If A_ij=u_i+v_j, then F_l=l(max X_l+max Y_l), with the same time bound. Additive separability is recognized by A_ij=A_i1+A_1j-A_11.

results.claim: If r rows and c columns are nonzero, there is an exact direct algorithm using O(mn+q min(rn,cm)) word operations; in particular, a constant number of nonzero rows or columns admits O(mn) time even with signed entries.
results.proof_sketch: Scan the matrix in O(mn), list its nonzero rows in order, and build a prefix sum for each such row. Fix a side l. A nonzero row h is included by vertical top a exactly for integer a in I_h=[max(0,h-l+1),min(h,m-l)]. The starts and one-past-ends of these clipped intervals are each nondecreasing with h, so merge them into an O(r)-event sweep over 0<=a<=m-l, grouping equal coordinates. Maintain, for every horizontal start b, T_b equal to the sum of the length-l row windows over the currently active rows. At each event coordinate x, apply all additions and removals to obtain the active set at x, then scan the T_b values and retain their maximum and coordinates; if no event occurs at zero, first scan the empty state realized at a=0. Each row event updates every T_b in O(n) via its row prefix. Between events the active set is unchanged, so this visits every realizable vertical state and computes F_l exactly in O(rn), with a baseline O(n) absorbed by O(mn) over all l. Initialize the best value below all integers: a genuinely empty active state contributes zero, whereas an all-negative state must remain negative. Repeating for q=min(m,n) sides costs O(mn+r n q). Transposing gives O(mn+c m q); choose the smaller method. Finally return the largest l with F_l<=k, or 0. Since q<=m,n, constant r or constant c makes the bound O(mn).

results.claim: A thresholded max-plus-convolution scan embeds exactly into matrices supported on one row.
results.proof_sketch: Given integer vectors x,y of length N, define c_t=max_{i+j=t}(x_i+y_j). Put W=max(1,max|x_i|,max|y_j|), C=2W+1, H=C+W+1, and B=4N. Define a prefix sequence p_0,...,p_B as follows: p_s=H for 0<=s<=2N-2, p_s=-H for 2N+2<=s<=B, and set the three intervening values arbitrarily. Overwrite p_i=-x_i and p_{B-j}=y_j+C. Form a B by B matrix whose first row is p_{s+1}-p_s and whose other rows are zero. For l=B-t, 0<=t<=2N-2, every relevant horizontal start satisfies s<=t. If s=i<N and j=t-i lies in [0,N-1], its window sum is C+x_i+y_j. Every other such window sum is negative by the choice of H, while a valid sum is at least one. Squares avoiding the first row have sum zero. Consequently F_{B-t}=C+c_t exactly. With threshold C+K, if some c_t<=K, the answer is B minus the least such t; otherwise it is below B-(2N-2). Thus the signed problem contains a precise convolutional primitive on one-row inputs.

results.claim: Any single-matrix reduction that represents N distinct source indices by N distinct positive side lengths must create a matrix with at least N^2 explicit cells.
results.proof_sketch: An m by n matrix offers exactly q=min(m,n) positive square side lengths. If N source indices are decoded from N distinct lengths of that one matrix, then q>=N. Since m>=q and n>=q, necessarily mn>=q^2>=N^2. The inherited max-plus construction uses this length-indexed decoding with B=4N and therefore lies on the quadratic side of this unavoidable size bound. Consequently, even an O(mn) matrix algorithm would give only an O(N^2) algorithm through that construction. This is a limitation of the stated reduction template, not a lower bound against other reductions and not evidence that the unrestricted word-RAM endpoint is impossible.

results.claim: If integer bit lengths are unbounded and bit operations are charged, an O(mn) bound independent of bit length is impossible.
results.proof_sketch: For a 1 by 1 matrix, the answer is determined by comparing its entry with k. On the explicit-binary bit-cost model, take a=k=2^(B-1). For every lower position r, replacing a by k+2^r changes the correct answer while changing only that bit. On the equality input a deterministic correct algorithm must inspect all B-1 lower positions, since otherwise the corresponding alternative is indistinguishable. Thus comparison has worst-case cost Omega(B), and no uniform O(mn)=O(1) bit-time bound exists even in this base case. The open algorithmic endpoint therefore only makes sense under a unit-cost word-RAM assumption or a stated bound on entry bit length. This does not rule out O(mn) word operations.

final_writeup:
Let q=min(m,n) and F_l denote the maximum sum among all l by l squares. I did not obtain either a general O(mn) word-RAM algorithm or a standard fine-grained lower bound excluding one, so the main endpoint remains unresolved.

There is also a matching input-reading lower bound in the standard explicit one-word-per-entry model. On the all-zero Boolean matrix with k=0 the answer is q, but changing any single cell to one makes q infeasible because every cell lies in some q-square. A deterministic exact algorithm must therefore probe all mn cells on the zero input. Thus O(mn), if achieved, would be optimal in this model; this does not show that the endpoint is impossible.

The strongest general positive result is a linear verifier. A proposed answer L is correct exactly when every L-square has sum at most k and, for each l>L, one supplied l-square has sum greater than k. A two-dimensional prefix table verifies all of this in O(mn) time. This also yields a simple exact descending search taking O(mnq) worst-case time, with a sharper output-sensitive bound when L is close to q. The L=0 case certifies that every positive length has an explicit violation.

Signed matrices present a genuine structural obstruction: feasibility need not be monotone and can alternate for every consecutive side length. The matrix with first row 1,-1,1,-1,... and all remaining entries zero has F_l=1 for odd l and F_l=0 for even l. Thus binary search, monotone pruning, and the paper's no-revisit reasoning cannot extend directly. A separate 2 by 3 example shows that merely decreasing the current length and continuing the scan can miss a violation at an earlier position.

There are nevertheless broad signed special cases attaining the endpoint. Multiplicatively rank-one matrices and additively separable matrices can both be recognized and solved in O(mn) exact arithmetic. Their square sums separate into products or sums of one-dimensional window sums, whose extrema over all lengths require q(m+n)<=2mn work. For a negative rank-one pivot, each of the four corner numerators is divided by the pivot before their maximum is taken, avoiding an inequality-direction error.

A new direct event sweep gives a further parameterized class. If r rows are nonzero, then for fixed l each supported row is active over one interval of vertical top coordinates. Across all vertical placements only O(r) active sets occur. Maintaining every horizontal length-l window total through the interval endpoints computes F_l in O(rn), so all sides cost O(mn+r n q). Transposition gives O(mn+c m q) for c nonzero columns, and the better orientation gives O(mn+q min(rn,cm)). This is O(mn) whenever the number of nonzero rows or columns is constant, and more generally when r q=O(m) or c q=O(n). The construction handles simultaneous boundary events, empty placements, and all-negative maxima without monotonicity.

Finally, the one-row construction shows that high-side-length maxima can encode max-plus-convolution coefficients exactly. It isolates a concrete convolutional core that a general solution must handle, although it does not itself preclude O(mn). Indeed, any one-instance reduction decoding N source indices from N distinct side lengths needs q>=N and hence mn>=N^2 explicit cells. The construction's quadratic blow-up is therefore unavoidable for that length-indexed template, and the sparse-support algorithm merely realizes the corresponding quadratic scan within the input bound.

Under literal bit complexity, unbounded integers already make O(mn) impossible for a 1 by 1 input. This is only the generic input-length obstruction. The substantive unrestricted bounded-word/unit-cost endpoint remains open.
